name: us-state-tax
description: Dependency-free US state AND LOCAL individual income tax engine for tax years 2025 and 2026, covering 33 states and 1,033 local income taxes. Models what rate tables leave out. MISSOURI, where ONE DOLLAR OF INCOME COSTS $61.94: Mo. Rev. Stat. 143.171.2 deducts a SHARE of the federal income tax and writes the share as a CLIFF rather than a phase-out - 35% of the whole bill at $25,000 or less of Missouri AGI, 25% to $50,000, 15% to $100,000, 5% to $125,000 and nothing above - so crossing a boundary moves the entire deduction down a step at once and the engine's own marginal-rate field reports 61.946 at $100,000 against 0.047 a thousand dollars either side, a figure no table of Missouri's rates can contain because the number falling off the cliff belongs to a different government; the FIRST STATE IN THE UNITED STATES TO EXEMPT CAPITAL GAINS OUTRIGHT, by HB 594 signed 10 July 2025 and retroactive to 1 January, SHORT-TERM GAINS INCLUDED where Massachusetts at the other end of this package charges them 8.5% - and the exemption is worth MORE than the rate times the gain, because it is a subtraction in arriving at MISSOURI AGI, the very figure the cliff chart is read against, so it takes the gain out of the base AND moves the filer down a step: $2,960.79 on a $60,000 gain where 4.7% of the gain alone is $2,820; where the $5,000/$10,000 cap on that deduction was DEAD LAW from 2019 to 2024 because 35% of a federal bill reaches $5,000 only at $14,286 of tax and nobody with $25,000 of Missouri AGI pays that, and the capital gains exemption revived it - while the same chart bounds how much it can ever be worth, at most $181.68 for a single filer and nothing at all for a couple, whose $32,200 standard deduction already exceeds the $25,000 the 35% step allows; where the WORKING FAMILY TAX CREDIT is 20% of the federal earned income credit and non-refundable, zeroing most low-income Missouri returns outright - a head of household with one teenager on $35,000 of wages owes $264.22 before it and nothing after - and is lost ENTIRELY above $4,400 of investment income, a limit that is a CONFORMITY DATE rather than a figure Missouri chose, because 143.177.3(1) reads section 32 as it stood on 1 January 2021 and the pre-ARPA disqualified income ceiling is several times lower than today's, so a filer with $5,000 of investment income keeps the whole federal credit and loses the whole state one; where the federal earned income credit is therefore read TWICE IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, subtracted from the federal tax deduction by the MO-1040 line 9 worksheet and matched at a fifth by 143.177, which no other state here does; where the EIGHT BRACKETS ARE ONE NUMBER, the first band's width times one through seven under the 143.011.5 block indexation - $1,348 for 2026, $1,313 for 2025, the first band taxed at ZERO and 4.7% beginning at $9,436 - which makes the whole graduated schedule worth $180.63 against a flat rate, and it does NOT double on a joint return because the brackets do not change at all; where A RETIREE'S SOCIAL SECURITY EATS THEIR PUBLIC PENSION EXEMPTION, because Form MO-A Part 3 Section A caps the public pension deduction at the maximum Social Security benefit ($47,633 for 2025) and then SUBTRACTS the Section C Social Security deduction, so $70,000 of public pension alone deducts $47,633 and the same $70,000 as $40,000 of pension plus $30,000 of taxable benefit deducts $40,000 - $7,633 apart on identical income in a state that taxes neither kind of it - while Section B's private pension deduction on the SAME FORM takes that benefit back OUT of the income its $6,000-a-person allowance is tested against, so one dollar of Social Security destroys a dollar of public pension exemption and protects a dollar of private pension one; where that $6,000 is withdrawn DOLLAR FOR DOLLAR above $25,000 ($32,000 joint), doubling the marginal rate to 9.4% inside the band; where military retired pay is exempt in full at any age outside both ceilings; and where the two states here that deduct the federal income tax SUBTRACT DIFFERENT REFUNDABLE CREDITS - Alabama's worksheet takes the refundable child tax credit and Missouri's starts from Form 1040 line 22, which line 28 never reduced, so $1,600 of it costs an Alabama family $80 and a Missouri family nothing. ALABAMA, the only state here whose tax base contains the FEDERAL TAX BILL: Form 40 line 12 deducts the federal income tax paid and EVERY filer takes it, not only itemizers, so a federal tax cut is an Alabama tax increase of 5% of the cut - a $2,200 child tax credit costs an Alabama family $110 of state tax, and the federal earned income credit RAISES Alabama tax because the worksheet subtracts the refundable credits too, so the same input moves the answer in opposite directions in two of this package's states; where the 5% top rate begins at $3,000 of taxable income and has since 1935, making the whole graduated schedule worth $40 against a flat 5%; where the standard deduction is a staircase that rounds the OPPOSITE way from Connecticut's - $25 per $500 of Alabama AGI above $25,500 with no 'or fraction thereof', so the first $499 cost nothing where Connecticut's first dollar costs the whole step - and every column reaches its floor at $35,500 in exactly twenty steps, the separate column's $88 being $87.50 rounded up so its twentieth step is worth $78; where ONE dependent exemption chart serves all five filing statuses, so two single parents at $50,000 each claim $1,000 a child and the same two people jointly on $100,000 claim $500; and where retirement turns on the TYPE OF PLAN rather than the person or the money - a defined BENEFIT payment is exempt in full at any age with no cap under Ala. Admin. Code r. 810-3-19-.04, while a defined CONTRIBUTION distribution is taxed above $6,000 and only from 65, so at 62 a $60,000 pension is free and a $60,000 401(k) draw costs $2,760.00 and nothing on a federal return tells the two apart. Alabama also exempted overtime before Congress did and stopped the month Congress started: the whole overtime wage, uncapped, to 30 June 2025, then the premium only and capped at $1,000 for 2026-2028. CONNECTICUT, where there is no continuous stretch of income tax above $30,000 because four staircases overlap and three of them are built from the same four words of statute - 'or fraction thereof' - so each is reached by ONE DOLLAR of extra income rather than by a proportion of it: the personal exemption is withdrawn $1,000 for each $1,000 above $30,000, DOLLAR FOR DOLLAR, so the marginal rate between $30,000 and $45,000 is exactly DOUBLE the statutory one (9% in a 4.5% bracket, a figure that appears in no table because it is two rules meeting) and the first dollar over each thousand costs $45; the 2% rate phase-out adds back $25 per $5,000 above $56,500 to a maximum of $250; the tax recapture adds $25, $90 and $50 per $5,000 above $105,000, $200,000 and $500,000 to a total of $3,400; and the personal tax credit falls from 75% to 1% of the whole tax over 27 steps whose boundary belongs to the step BELOW it, because section 12-703 reads 'over $15,000 but not over $18,800' while the 2023 pension phase-out on the SAME return reads 'at least $75,000 but less than $77,500' and belongs to the step above - two opposite conventions, one return. Half of Connecticut's tables scale between filing statuses and half do not, and the two halves look identical: the rate schedule and the recapture are the joint figures times one half (single and separate) or four fifths (head of household), with ONE exception a test written from the statute caught - a head of household's MIDDLE recapture tier is $140 per $8,000 to a maximum of $4,200 where four fifths would be $144 and $4,320 - while the exemption, the add-back thresholds and the credit do not scale at all, and the figures a scaling model produces ($12,000 of exemption, a $50,250 add-back threshold) are REAL Connecticut numbers belonging to a SEPARATE filer, so the error survives a plausibility check. Connecticut's Social Security subtraction is a cliff and stays one: below $75,000 ($100,000 joint) of federal AGI the whole taxable benefit comes out, and at the threshold it is replaced rather than tapered by 25% of the lesser of gross benefits and the section 86 combined income excess - $405 of tax on one dollar of income for a couple with $40,000 of benefits. And 2026 is the FIRST year a Connecticut retiree's traditional IRA is treated like their pension, because the IRA subtraction phases in 25/50/75/100 over 2023-2026: it is the only Connecticut figure that differs between the two years here. No county, city or town levies an income tax. VIRGINIA, whose four printed brackets are worth exactly $257.50 to every filer at every income forever, because the 5.75% top rate begins at $17,000 of taxable income for a single filer AND at $17,000 on a joint return and has since 1990 - so the Commonwealth's published $259 ceiling on the spouse tax adjustment is $1.50 above the largest figure its own worksheet can produce and has never once bound; where the age deduction is withdrawn DOLLAR FOR DOLLAR above $50,000 ($75,000 joint) of adjusted federal AGI, so a couple who are both 65 pay $2,760 of tax on $24,000 of income - 11.5%, twice the state's top rate, and a figure that appears in no table because it is two rules meeting; where that test reads federal AGI LESS taxable Social Security while the deduction comes off Virginia AGI, a gap worth $2,572.80 to a retired couple on $90,000; where a filer born on or before 1 January 1939 is not income-tested at all, so the provision sunsets by mortality; where TWO poverty floors set by two different governments mean the cliff is $168.55 for a single filer, $106.23 for a childless couple and $416.55 for a family of four - and vanishes entirely for the same family if they claim the federal earned income credit, because Virginia's 20% match and its $300-a-head Credit for Low Income Individuals are alternatives and only one is refundable; and where NO county, city or town levies an income tax at all. Ohio, whose printed schedule is DISCONTINUOUS - a filer with $26,050 of taxable nonbusiness income owes nothing and one with $26,050.01 owes $342.00, because O.R.C. 5747.02(A)(3) charges the constant whole on the first dollar of the band, so reading the three rows as marginal brackets understates every Ohio filer by $342 - and which steps a SECOND time by $18.69 at $100,000 because HB 96 re-based the lower constant from $360.69 to $342.00 and left the upper one at what $360.69 chained to; where the first $250,000 of business income is deducted and the excess taxed at a flat 3%, so $250,000 of Schedule C profit costs $0 and $250,000 of wages costs $7,022.45; where the exemption chart and every credit limit are read against a modified AGI that adds the business deduction straight back; where the $20 exemption credit is claimable ONLY by a childless single filer in a $1,550 window of income and the joint filing credit's 20% row is unreachable arithmetic; and where 679 municipalities charge 0.45% to 3.00% on QUALIFYING WAGES - box 5 of the W-2, which a 401(k) deferral does not reduce, costing a Columbus saver $612.50 a year that box 1 never shows - so the municipal tax is the LARGER half of every Ohio return below $126,408.32 of income, an Ohio retiree owes their municipality nothing, and a commuter pays the higher of the two rates whichever way they commute because Ohio has no statutory resident credit and no half rate for nonresidents; Michigan, where Detroit charges residents 2.4% on a base the MI-1040 does not contain, where the personal exemption has been the $600 the Legislature set in 1964 and is worth $14.40 against an indexed $5,800 state exemption, and where a Lansing resident commuting to Detroit pays 70% more city tax than one working at home; Indiana, where the average county rate is 1.914% against a state rate of 3.00%; MARYLAND, which TAXES SOCIAL SECURITY AND EXEMPTS PENSIONS - the state does not tax the benefit and then charges the whole of it, taxable or not, against the pension exclusion dollar for dollar, so $30,000 of benefits plus $60,000 of pension and $90,000 of pension alone reach the same Maryland AGI to the cent and a dollar of benefit adds a FULL dollar to the base while a dollar of pension adds nothing; where that exclusion is claimed PER PERSON so a return's totals do not determine its tax - one couple with $80,000 of pension and $40,000 of benefits pays $720.00, $758.40 or $3,261.65 depending only on whose name the income is in; where an IRA is NOT an employee retirement system, so the rollover every adviser recommends costs a retiree $3,428.03 a year at $150,000 with nothing on the federal return to show it happened; where military retired pay has NO age gate at all and the first $100,000 of a centenarian's income comes off whatever it is; where the maximum exclusion FALLS in 2026, the only parameter here that has ever gone down; where every resident owes a county income tax of 2.25%-3.30%, where Frederick County's bracket selects one rate that applies to the WHOLE income so one dollar at $150,000 costs $360.03, and where the new 2% capital gains surtax is a test rather than a floor so one dollar of AGI at $350,000 can cost $6,933.08; GEORGIA, whose retirement income exclusion is the MIRROR IMAGE of Maryland's and is never described that way: it is measured on the CHARACTER of the income - interest, dividends, net capital gain, rents, royalties, alimony, pensions AND taxable IRA distributions all qualify in full - and nothing is charged against it, so rolling a 401(k) into an IRA costs a Georgia retiree nothing where the same rollover costs a Marylander $3,378.83 a year, and moving a third of a retirement into Social Security SAVES $1,272.45 in Georgia and COSTS $357.75 in Maryland, in two states that both say they do not tax the benefit; where at most $5,000 of a person's wages may enter the exclusion, so at 65 a filer with $65,000 of dividends owes nothing and one with $65,000 of wages owes $2,245.50 on identical income; where net capital gain is in the pool and the allowance is annual and per person, making the 'retirement income exclusion' a CAPITAL GAINS ALLOWANCE that lets a couple both 65 realise $130,000 of gain a year tax-free; where the military exclusion of $17,500 plus $17,500 is available only BELOW 62 and its second half is a cliff on employment, so one dollar of wages at $17,500 is worth $873.20; and where composing the two exclusions gives a true maximum of $70,000 rather than the $65,000 every table prints - for a disabled veteran under 62, whose exclusion then FALLS by half on their sixty-second birthday, the birthday every guide calls the one where Georgia's exclusion begins. Massachusetts, which every rate table reports as a flat 5% and which taxes short-term capital gains at 8.5%; New Jersey, whose retirement exclusion ends in a wall that costs a joint retiree $1,381 on one dollar; CalEITC, which is a triangle with no plateau; New York City's 3.078%-3.876% resident tax and its 30%-to-10% sliding earned income credit; the Yonkers surcharge of 16.75% of the state tax; which federal figure each state starts from; which federal deductions it adds back; and the credit phase-outs that make Utah's and Pennsylvania's flat taxes anything but flat. Every figure cited to the statute or state release it came from, and every carried-forward figure flagged as provisional. KENTUCKY, whose published $31,110 pension exclusion is neither its maximum nor its shape: retired pay from the federal government, the Commonwealth or a Kentucky local government - military service included - is exempt IN FULL to the extent it is attributable to service performed before 1 January 1998, with NO CEILING, and that exemption does not consume the $31,110, which stays available against everything else, so a teacher who served 1975-2005 with a $70,000 pension and a $40,000 IRA excludes $84,776.67 on a return whose published exclusion is $31,110; where there is NO AGE TEST AT ALL, so of the three states here that exempt retirement income Kentucky has the smallest headline figure and is the only one an early retiree can use - at 55 a couple with $70,000 of pension pays $157.85 in Kentucky, $1,996.00 in Georgia and $4,471.05 in Montgomery County, and at 65 the ranking REVERSES and Kentucky is the only one of the three that charges anything; where Kentucky asks nothing about the character of the income or the form of the account, so the rollover that costs a Marylander $3,428.03 a year costs a Kentuckian nothing; and where the 1998 cutoff has never moved, so the cohort is closed, every further month of service dilutes the exempt percentage, and two teachers with identical pensions pay $1,878.33 apart on the decade they worked. UTAH, whose 4.45% flat tax is a 15.26% marginal rate on a retiree - 3.4 times the statutory rate and three rules compounding with no bracket among them: section 86 puts $1.85 of taxable income behind each dollar of pension, Utah taxes all of it, and TWO credits are withdrawn against it at once, 2.5 cents of Social Security Benefits Credit and 1.3 cents of Taxpayer Tax Credit - so the rate runs 10.64% to 15.26% to 8.25% as income rises and the highest-taxed next dollar in Utah belongs to a household in the 12% FEDERAL bracket; where the state taxes the benefit and hands the whole tax back as a credit below $90,000 of modified AGI, making Social Security free and then charging 2.5% on every dollar of anything else; where tax-exempt interest is added back for that test, so a municipal bond is taxed at 2.5% while appearing on no line of Utah income and costs $250 on $10,000 with no federal change at all; where the three retirement credits are an ELECTION under section 59-10-1019(5) - code 18, or codes AH and AJ, never both - and code 18 is all but dead law, worth at most $395.00 across a $22,600 window, only to filers born on or before 31 December 1952, and only where there is no Social Security at all; and where the military retirement credit is DEFINED as the rate by cross-reference rather than stored as a number, so it moved when the rate did.
